title: XQC: Well-conditioned Optimization Accelerates Deep Reinforcement Learning
claim: A method with well-conditioned optimization matches or beats larger baselines on return while being far smaller and cheaper.
layout: 4 panels, left-to-right, shared color-coded legend underneath
description: A wide strip of four plots sharing one color legend along the bottom, with the proposed method XQC in hot pink. Panel 1 is a scatter of IQM condition number (log scale) against IQM return at 1M steps, with labeled dots for SAC, CrossQ, CrossQ+WN, SimbaV2 and XQC. XQC sits lowest, with the smallest condition number and the highest return. Panel 2 is a bar chart of parameter counts. XQC's bar is the smallest and the BRC bar is the tallest, at about 35M. Panel 3 is a bar chart of IQM AUC return over 55 state-based tasks with error bars. XQC is highest at 0.73. Panel 4 is a learning curve for pixel-based humanoid-walk, where XQC's pink curve rises faster than the grey DrQ-V2 curve. The eye goes first to the pink elements.
caption: Well-conditioned network architectures yield state-of-the-art RL performance. Our algorithm, XQC with a BN and WN-based architecture and a CE loss, achieves competitive performance against state-of-the-art baselines across 55 proprioceptive continuous control tasks from four different benchmarks with a single set of hyperparameters. Notably, with ∼4.5× fewer parameters and ∼5× less compute in terms of FLOP/S than SIMBA-V2, the closest competitor. XQC’s efficiency carries over to RL from pixels on 15 vision-based DMC tasks, significantly improving on DRQ-V2.
abstract: Sample efficiency is a central property of effective deep reinforcement learning algorithms. Recent work has improved this through added complexity, such as larger models, exotic network architectures, and more complex algorithms, which are typically motivated purely by empirical performance. We take a more principled approach by focusing on the optimization landscape of the critic network. Using the eigenspectrum and condition number of the critic's Hessian, we systematically investigate the impact of common architectural design decisions on training dynamics. Our analysis reveals that a novel combination of batch normalization (BN), weight normalization (WN), and a distributional cross-entropy (CE) loss produces condition numbers orders of magnitude smaller than baselines. This combination also naturally bounds gradient norms, a property critical for maintaining a stable effective learning rate under non-stationary targets and bootstrapping. Based on these insights, we introduce XQC: a well-motivated, sample-efficient deep actor-critic algorithm built upon soft actor-critic that embodies these optimization-aware principles. We achieve state-of-the art sample efficiency across 55 proprioception and 15 vision-based continuous control tasks, all while using significantly fewer parameters than competing methods. Our code is available at danielpalenicek.github.io/projects/xqc.
